core_territory: Valley of Mexico; Puebla-Tlaxcala; Toluca; Morelos
domain_territory: Michoacan; Oaxaca; Hidalgo; Queretaro; Guanajuato; central Veracruz coast
sphere_territory: The Bajio; Gulf lowlands; north toward the Aridoamerican frontier; south toward the Maya zone
anchor_cities: Mexico City; Puebla; Toluca; Oaxaca; Morelia; Veracruz
founding_population: Sedentary maize civilizations of central and southern Mexico - Nahua, Mixtec, Zapotec, Totonac, Purepecha, Huastec - conquered not displaced from 1519
characteristic_institution: Encomienda over an existing tribute system, then congregacion, then hacienda
notes: Mexico held ~17.2M people in 1492, about 37% of the hemisphere's Indigenous population. Northern border must stop short of La Republica de Sonora, which holds only Sonora and Chihuahua (plus Arizona and New Mexico). IMPORTANT: Coahuila, Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas belong to NO nation and are in scope - they carry Monterrey, AHMSA, the Sabinas coal basin, the Burgos gas basin and the Comarca Lagunera, and are a live candidate either for this region or for a separate norteno polity.

modern_countries: Guatemala; Mexico; Belize; Honduras; El Salvador
core_territory: Totonicapan; Solola; El Quiche; Alta Verapaz; Huehuetenango
domain_territory: Rest of the Guatemalan highlands; Chiapas highlands; the Peten
sphere_territory: Guatemala's Pacific piedmont; western Belize; western Honduran and Salvadoran fringe
anchor_cities: Quetzaltenango; Coban; Huehuetenango; San Cristobal de las Casas; Flores
founding_population: Maya peoples of the Chiapas and Guatemalan highlands - 22 distinct Mayan-language nations in Guatemala alone - conquered late and only partially
characteristic_institution: Encomienda and repartimiento over intact village polities, then the coffee finca
notes: Guatemala's 2018 census: 43.43% Indigenous nationally, but 98.0% in Totonicapan, 96.4% in Solola, 93.0% in Alta Verapaz, 89.2% in El Quiche. Contiguous Indigenous-majority blocks.

modern_countries: Guatemala; El Salvador; Honduras; Nicaragua; Costa Rica
core_territory: Volcanic Pacific slope and central valleys: all of El Salvador; Guatemalan piedmont; central Honduras; Nicaragua's Pacific lowland; Costa Rica's Central Valley
domain_territory: The interior highlands behind the Pacific slope
sphere_territory: Transition zones toward the Caribbean side and the Maya highlands
anchor_cities: San Salvador; Tegucigalpa; Managua; San Jose; Leon; Granada
founding_population: Spanish-and-mestizo (ladino) society on a thinner, less organized Indigenous base than Mesoamerica or the Maya highlands
characteristic_institution: The finca and the cattle hacienda; coffee from the mid-19th century, with land privatization dissolving communal holdings
notes: Costa Rica is a standing exception - a genuinely smallholder coffee frontier with a weaker oligarchy, earlier franchise and better public provision. May belong with the Euro-American tier or stand alone. The most artificial entry in the list; partly defined by what it is not.

modern_countries: Nicaragua; Honduras; Belize; Panama; Colombia; Venezuela; Guatemala
core_territory: Nicaraguan and Honduran Caribbean coast; Belize; the Garifuna coast from Belize through Honduras
domain_territory: Panama's Caribbean side and Kuna territory; Colombia's Caribbean coast; Venezuela's Caribbean littoral
sphere_territory: The whole Caribbean basin, overlapping region 5
anchor_cities: Bluefields; Puerto Cabezas; Belize City; La Ceiba; Colon; Cartagena; Barranquilla
founding_population: Tri-partite: surviving Indigenous coastal peoples, Afro-descended populations arriving by several routes, and a thin mostly non-Iberian European presence
characteristic_institution: Not the Spanish system at all - English and Dutch commercial and buccaneering contact, logwood and mahogany, later the banana enclave
notes: A rim, not a bloc: a 2000km arc of enclaves with sea between them, which strains the core/domain/sphere model. Miskito Kingdom allied with Britain from 1638, annexed only in 1894. Nicaragua's autonomous regions RACCN and RACCS are formal recognition of the separateness.

modern_countries: Cuba; Haiti; Dominican Republic; Jamaica; Puerto Rico; Barbados; Trinidad and Tobago; the Leewards and Windwards; Martinique; Guadeloupe
core_territory: The sugar islands: Barbados; Jamaica; Haiti; western Cuba's plantation zone; Puerto Rico's coast; the Leewards and Windwards; Martinique; Guadeloupe
domain_territory: The rest of the Greater and Lesser Antilles
sphere_territory: The mainland rim (region 4); the Guianas (region 6); Brazil's Nordeste; and per Garreau, Miami
anchor_cities: Havana; Kingston; Port-au-Prince; Santo Domingo; San Juan; Bridgetown; Fort-de-France
founding_population: Overwhelmingly enslaved Africans and their descendants. The Indigenous population - ~3 million in 1492 - was destroyed within a century, earlier and more completely than anywhere else in the hemisphere
characteristic_institution: The sugar plantation, and nothing else comes close
notes: Cuba was at 167% and Barbados at 150% of US per-capita income in 1700; Barbados was at 51% by 1997. Of all migration to British colonies 1630-1780, the West Indies took 66% of the total and 83% of enslaved Africans. Treating the islands as one flattens the sharpest internal distinction in the survey - Haiti in particular is arguably its own object.

core_territory: The coastal polder strip of Guyana and Suriname
domain_territory: French Guiana's coast; the Maroon river territories of the Suriname interior
sphere_territory: The Guiana Shield interior; Amapa; Guayana Esequiba; the Orinoco delta
founding_population: The most compositionally complex founding stack in the Americas: Indigenous Arawakan and Cariban peoples, enslaved Africans, Maroon nations, indentured South Asians (a demographic plurality), Javanese, Chinese and Portuguese-Madeiran indenture
characteristic_institution: The Dutch polder plantation - sugar estates on drained coastal marsh - and the Maroon treaty
notes: The Ndyuka signed the first territorial-autonomy treaty with the Dutch on 10 October 1760; it still defines Maroon territorial rights today. Under two million people across all three territories. Everyone lives on a narrow coastal strip and the interior is effectively another country.

core_territory: The Peruvian sierra from Cajamarca to Cusco; the Ecuadorian inter-Andean corridor
domain_territory: The western slope toward the coastal valleys; the eastern slope toward the ceja de selva
sphere_territory: The Peruvian coast; the Colombian Andes; the upper Amazon
anchor_cities: Cusco; Quito; Huancayo; Ayacucho; Cajamarca; Riobamba
founding_population: Quechua-speaking agricultural and pastoral societies of the Peruvian and Ecuadorian sierra, organized by the Inca state at contact. The Andes held ~15.7 million people in 1492, second only to Mexico
characteristic_institution: Reduccion, then hacienda. Toledo resettled ~1.4 million people into ~840 planned grid towns between 1569 and 1575
notes: The towns people live in now are the ones Toledo laid out. Peru recorded 5.9 million Indigenous people in 2017. Splitting this from region 8 is contestable - most scholarship treats the Central Andes as one culture area.

core_territory: The Bolivian and southern Peruvian altiplano: La Paz; El Alto; Oruro; Puno; Potosi
domain_territory: The Bolivian valleys - Cochabamba, Sucre; northern Chile's and northwestern Argentina's high country
sphere_territory: The Pacific slope down to Arica and Iquique; the Yungas; the Chaco fringe
anchor_cities: La Paz; El Alto; Oruro; Potosi; Puno; Cochabamba
founding_population: Aymara-speaking societies of the high plateau around Lake Titicaca, with a pre-Inca state tradition - Tiwanaku, and Chiripa before it - that predates and was never fully absorbed by Cusco
characteristic_institution: The mita. The Toledo draft of 1573 pulled one-seventh of adult males from a catchment of nearly 200,000 square miles into Potosi and Huancavelica
notes: THE LAST MERGE TO MAKE, NOT THE FIRST. The mita boundary is still measurable: ~25% lower household consumption and 6 percentage points more child stunting inside it (Dell 2010). It follows no modern administrative line. Bolivia is 62% self-identified Indigenous. At ~3750m it is the most extensive high plateau on earth outside Tibet.

modern_countries: Brazil; Peru; Colombia; Ecuador; Bolivia; Venezuela; Guyana
core_territory: The main-stem Amazon and its major tributaries - Solimoes, Negro, Madeira, Tapajos, Xingu
domain_territory: The whole basin across Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia and Venezuela
sphere_territory: The Guiana Shield; the Llanos de Mojos; the ceja de selva; the Cerrado fringe
anchor_cities: Manaus; Belem; Iquitos; Santarem; Leticia; Porto Velho
founding_population: CONTESTED. Estimates now run from ~5 million to over 8 million in 1492, supported by engineered terra preta soils, the Marajoara mounds, Upper Xingu roads and planned plazas, and the Acre geoglyphs. Population fell to ~1 million by 1900 and under 200,000 by the early 1980s
characteristic_institution: None ever held. Missions, descimento slaving raids, the rubber boom, and the 1960s-70s road frontier are episodes, not founding settlements
notes: The one large region where first effective settlement arguably has not happened yet - or happened before 1492 and is currently being re-attempted. The wilderness Europeans described had already been depopulated by disease running ahead of them. May be a zone rather than a nation.

core_territory: The Venezuelan llanos, Apure to Guarico
sphere_territory: The Orinoco delta; the Andean piedmont; the Guiana Shield edge
anchor_cities: San Fernando de Apure; Calabozo; Villavicencio; Puerto Ayacucho
founding_population: Mixed Indigenous, African and European cattle-herding populations formed in the 17th and 18th centuries around missions and open-range ranching
characteristic_institution: Open-range cattle on unfenced savanna, worked by the llanero - the structural analogue of the gaucho and the vaquero
notes: THE WEAKEST OF THE THIRTEEN AND THE FIRST TO CUT. A way of life more than a founding society, with no measured institutional boundary. Could merge into region 4, into region 9's sphere, or be treated as one instance of a hemisphere-wide pastoral-frontier type.

core_territory: The humid pampas of Buenos Aires, Santa Fe, Entre Rios and Cordoba, plus all of Uruguay
domain_territory: The Argentine litoral and the Parana corridor
sphere_territory: Northwest Argentina (genuinely Andean, belongs to region 8's domain); Paraguay; Rio Grande do Sul; northern Patagonia
anchor_cities: Buenos Aires; Montevideo; Rosario; Cordoba; Santa Fe
founding_population: The clearest Povo Transplantado in the hemisphere: a thin Spanish colonial society on a sparse non-sedentary Indigenous base, followed by mass European immigration that effectively became the majority
characteristic_institution: The estancia - extensive cattle ranching on the pampas - later overlaid by grain export, refrigerated meat and a centralized port-capital economy
notes: Argentine literacy reached 45.6% by 1895 and 73% by 1925; Argentina stood at 102% of US per-capita income in 1800. But the voting share was 1.8% in 1896 and Patagonian landownership ran 6.6% to 35.2% - Euro-American in founding population, oligarchic in land tenure. Paraguay does not fit and is jammed into the sphere; it is the strongest candidate for a 14th region.

core_territory: The Central Valley from Santiago to Concepcion
domain_territory: Valparaiso; the Norte Chico; the near south
sphere_territory: The northern desert mining zone; Araucania to the south
founding_population: Spanish settlers on a moderately dense Mapuche and Picunche base, hemmed into a narrow Mediterranean-climate valley between the Atacama, the Andes and the Bio-Bio frontier
characteristic_institution: The hacienda with resident tenant labor, dismantled by land reform between 1962 and 1973; plus nitrate and copper mining in the north as a separate externally-capitalized economy
notes: The most geographically bounded society in the hemisphere - desert north, ocean west, Andes east, hostile frontier south - which produced unusually strong state capacity. Relative income held roughly steady (46% of the US in 1800, 42% in 1997) where Peru's and Mexico's fell by half or more.

core_territory: Araucania and Los Rios in Chile; Neuquen and Rio Negro in Argentina
domain_territory: The Chilean Lake District; Chiloe; Chubut
sphere_territory: Santa Cruz; Magallanes; Tierra del Fuego; the South Atlantic approaches
anchor_cities: Temuco; Valdivia; Bariloche; Neuquen; Punta Arenas; Ushuaia
founding_population: The Mapuche - the only people in the Americas to defeat both the Inca and the Spanish and hold a recognized frontier for three centuries. Plus Tehuelche, Selknam and Kawesqar of the far south, and post-1880 settler and immigrant populations
characteristic_institution: For three centuries the frontier itself - a negotiated, armed, trade-crossed boundary rather than a colonial administration. After 1883, military occupation and sheep estancias
notes: THE UNAVOIDABLE FINAL LEG of any route to the Falkland Islands - design it with that scene in mind. Chile's 2024 census records ~1.6 million Mapuche, 8.8% of the national population. A live territorial dispute with a 400-year record. Arguably two things bundled: a contested Indigenous homeland and an empty settler periphery.
